title: Biomass per recorded species made 77% of a nutrient contrast for novel plants in warmed tundra plots
abstract: We tested whether a nutrient contrast after seed addition came mainly from more recorded novel plant species or more biomass per recorded species. We used a public ten-year tundra experiment with 56 whole plots and paired seed subplots. In 28 warmed plots, added NPK raised the paired seed-addition response of novel biomass by 6.790 g per 25 x 25 cm subplot (95% bootstrap interval 3.438-10.514). The two-sided treatment-label p value was 0.000300. In seeded subplots, an exact split assigned 77.4% (68.2-90.5%) of the 6.809 g nutrient contrast to biomass per recorded species. A presence-based split assigned 87.9% to biomass among positive plots. Removal of any one warmed whole plot left the main intervention contrast positive. The warming difference in nutrient contrasts remained uncertain: 5.325 g (-3.257 to 14.989). The source paper already reported nutrient-dependent novel biomass and resident replacement. Our contribution is the quantified split, uncertainty and audit, not the discovery of resource limitation. One site, one endpoint year, group-level records and strong NPK addition limit inference. The split is not causal mediation and cannot separate species identity from growth. It does not estimate a nutrient share of the thermal-tracking gap. Code, aggregate results, a figure and exact external-data retrieval instructions are included.

display.caption: Novel plant biomass means and the warmed nutrient contrast. Nominal 95% intervals resample whole plots within the eight treatment cells. Recorded richness and biomass per species are exact components of the seeded contrast; the third estimate also uses paired unseeded subplots.
